newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE - Brazil council seen being more decisive.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE - Brazil council seen being more decisive.

text.p: The Brazilian government has paved the way for the creation of a new coffee council which unites private and public sectors to decide future policy and traders are optimistic its benefits will be felt long-term.

The council is not expected to introduce any radical changes but should guarantee action when it is needed after a period in which the international market has sometimes doubted Brazil's ability to take decisions.

"The moment the relationship between the private and the public sector is not clear, the tendency of the government has been not to take any decisions or measures," Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Federation, said.

"Instead of always defending, we (the private sector) have the chance of being on the attack, of making things happen. Now the government can also be confident that when something is approved, it has the support of the private sector," he added.
The government set the wheels in motion when on October 4 it published a decree allowing for the creation of a new coffee policy council to be known as the CPDC.
The council was suggested by a parliamentary committee which heard the views of key members from the private and public sector as how best to manage coffee policy in the future.
Up until now, decisions on coffee matters have been taken after consultations between government officials and the Brazilian Coffee Council (CBC), a private sector umbrella group.

However given that the CBC was only an informal body, decision making could be a lengthy process due to disagreements between the government and the private sector, within the private sector and even within individual entities.

"For the last years, the dynamics of the government/private sector relationship has been kept informal and inside a non-existing legal framework," said Francisco Ourique, executive director of Flavour Coffee.
Traders would like the council to tackle issues such as how to revive the country's coffee population and recover losses in world market share.

One other suggestion which could be discussed by the future council is the creation of a contribution tax to provide a fund to be used for promotional and other purposes, said Jair Coser, president of major exporter Unicafe.
"Why not have a tax of say $1 per 60-kg bag. In the end we would be investing in something we could reap the benefits of later," Coser said.

On the export market, prices had slipped from last week with Santos brokers Wolthers & Associates quoting speciality 17/18s coffees at 10 over New York for October/November shipment against last week's 13 point premium.
Fine 17/18s were six under against last week's four point discount and Swedish qualities had slipped to 14 from 10 under.
In the domestic market, Santos brokers Escritorio Carvalhaes on October 10 quoted fine-to-extrafine Mogiana/Minas green beans at 123/125 reais per 60 kg against the 119/121 reais quoted on October 4.
